We begin by defining the state of the power grid as a vector $\mathbf{x}_t$ representing the energization status of generators and transmission lines. A total blackout corresponds to the zero vector. The objective is to reach a target stable state $\mathbf{x}^*$ in minimal time. However, this greedy selection is strictly bounded by the `w4_stability_constraint_check`. If the proposed transition violates these inequalities, the `w4_corrective_action_feedback` loop activates, introducing a penalty term or forcing a load-shedding maneuver to project the state back into the feasible manifold. Furthermore, the `w4_black_start_topology` establishes the foundational boundary conditions. By partitioning the global graph into seven regional subgraphs, each anchored by an autonomous node (the black start unit), the high-dimensional search space is decomposed into tractable local optimizations. This hierarchical approach mirrors advanced control theory, specifically model predictive control (MPC), where a receding horizon is optimized subject to differential-algebraic equation constraints. The integration of virtual synchronous generators (VSG) further enriches this derivation by providing synthetic inertia, effectively smoothing the discrete jumps in the state-space trajectory and allowing for finer-grained control over the Rate of Change of Frequency (ROCOF). Thus, the restoration protocol is not merely a logistical checklist but a sophisticated application of constrained dynamical systems theory.
